questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a market in economics?
hints: Think about what a market does rather than what it looks like.
Check whether each option would still work for online trade or trade in resources such as labour.
questions.targets: A market is any arrangement for exchange, not only a physical place

options.text: A building where firms store goods before selling them
options.misconception: Storage is not exchange; a market is about buyers and sellers trading.

options.text: A place where buyers and sellers must meet face to face
options.misconception: Many markets, such as online markets, have no physical meeting place.

options.text: Any arrangement that links buyers and sellers so that they can carry out an exchange
A government agency that decides the prices of goods
options.misconception: In a market, prices come from buyers and sellers interacting, not from a government agency.

questions.prompt: Define the term demand.
hints: Think about the consumer side of a market and the demand curve.
Your definition should say what consumers must be able to do, and what conditions the curve is drawn under.
questions.targets: Willing and able; range of prices; time period; ceteris paribus
marking_points: The quantities of a good or service that consumers are willing and able to buy [1]
At different possible prices over a given time period, ceteris paribus [1]
questions.model_answer_note: Full marks need 'willing and able' plus the idea of different prices over a time period with other things constant.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a feature of a competitive market?
hints: Think about the number of buyers and sellers in a competitive market.
Ask whether any one buyer or seller could change the market price on their own.
questions.targets: Many buyers and sellers, none with power over price

options.text: A single firm sets the market price
options.misconception: One firm setting price describes market power, which competitive markets lack.

options.text: Buyers and sellers must trade in a single physical location
options.misconception: Location does not define competition; markets can be spread out or online.

options.text: Each firm sells a product very different from its rivals'
options.misconception: Very different products give firms some power over price, which does not fit a competitive market.

options.text: There are many buyers and sellers, so none can influence the price alone

questions.prompt: Define the term nudge.
hints: This term comes from behavioural economics and choice architecture.
Say what a nudge tries to change, and what tools it avoids using.
questions.targets: Influence choices predictably without incentives, penalties or removing options
marking_points: A way of influencing people's choices in a predictable (usually socially desirable) direction by changing how options are presented [1]
Without using financial incentives or penalties and without removing any options (freedom of choice is kept) [1]
questions.model_answer_note: Full marks need both the aim of influencing choices and the fact that freedom of choice is kept without incentives or bans.

questions.prompt: In Veld, tea and coffee are substitutes. The price of tea rises. What happens in the market for coffee?
hints: Use the idea of substitute goods as a non-price determinant of demand.
Think about what tea drinkers do when tea becomes dearer, then decide whether coffee's own price has changed.
questions.targets: Change in the price of a related good shifts the demand curve

options.text: There is a movement up along the demand curve for coffee
options.misconception: A movement along the curve needs a change in coffee's own price, which has not happened.

options.text: The demand curve for coffee shifts to the right
The demand curve for coffee shifts to the left
options.misconception: Demand shifts left when the price of a complement rises, not a substitute.

options.text: The supply curve for coffee shifts to the right
options.misconception: The price of tea affects coffee buyers, so it is a demand change, not a supply change.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would shift the supply curve of rice in Kuva to the right?
hints: Use the non-price determinants of supply.
Rule out anything that changes the price of rice itself or affects buyers, then ask which change lowers producers' costs.
questions.targets: Non-price determinants of supply vs price changes and demand factors

options.text: A rise in the price of rice
options.misconception: A change in the good's own price causes a movement along the supply curve, not a shift.

options.text: An increase in consumer incomes
options.misconception: Income is a determinant of demand, not supply.

options.text: A rise in the wages paid to rice farm workers
options.misconception: Higher costs reduce supply, shifting the curve to the left.

options.text: A fall in the price of fertiliser

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a normal good and an inferior good.
hints: Use consumer income as a determinant of demand.
For each type of good, describe what happens to demand when income goes up.
questions.targets: Direction of the income effect on demand
marking_points: For a normal good, demand increases when consumer income rises [1]
For an inferior good, demand decreases when consumer income rises [1]
questions.model_answer_note: Full marks need both goods with the direction of the demand change for a rise (or fall) in income.

questions.prompt: Table 1 shows the only three consumers of juice in a small market in Tarsa. What is the market quantity demanded at a price of 4 zeds?

table.caption: Table 1: Individual demand for juice (bottles per week)

hints: Use the row in Table 1 for a price of 4 zeds.
Market demand is built by adding across consumers at one price only.
questions.targets: Horizontal summation of individual demand

options.text: 3 bottles
options.misconception: This is only Consumer X's quantity, not the market total.

options.text: 10 bottles
17 bottles
options.misconception: This is the market quantity at a price of 2 zeds, not 4 zeds.

options.text: 27 bottles
options.misconception: This adds quantities at both prices; market demand adds consumers at one price only.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a movement along a demand curve and a shift of a demand curve.
hints: Think about what is measured on the axes of a demand diagram and what is held constant.
For each case, name the kind of change that causes it and what happens to the quantity bought.
questions.targets: Own-price change vs non-price determinant
marking_points: A movement along the curve is caused by a change in the good's own price, giving a change in quantity demanded [1]
A shift is caused by a change in a non-price determinant (e.g. income, tastes, prices of related goods), so a different quantity is demanded at every price [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer gives the cause of each and makes clear that a shift changes demand at every price.

questions.prompt: In a free market for bus passes in Veld, the price is currently below the equilibrium price. What is the situation and what will happen next?
hints: Compare quantity demanded and quantity supplied at a price below equilibrium on a demand and supply diagram.
Decide whether there is a shortage or a surplus, then think about how buyers and sellers react.
questions.targets: Disequilibrium below equilibrium price and the adjustment process

options.text: There is excess demand, so the price tends to rise
There is excess supply, so the price tends to fall
options.misconception: Excess supply happens when the price is above equilibrium, not below.

options.text: There is excess demand, so the price tends to fall
options.misconception: A shortage leads buyers to compete for the good, which pushes the price up, not down.

options.text: The market is in equilibrium because buyers and sellers are still trading
options.misconception: Trade happening does not mean quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.

questions.prompt: Table 2 shows the demand and supply schedules for mangoes in Kuva. (a) Identify the equilibrium price and quantity. (b) Calculate the excess demand at a price of 4 zeds.

table.caption: Table 2: Market for mangoes in Kuva (thousand per week)

hints: Use the condition for market equilibrium and the row for 4 zeds in Table 2.
Find the row where the two quantities match, then at 4 zeds subtract the smaller quantity from the larger one.
questions.targets: Reading equilibrium from a schedule and measuring a shortage
marking_points: Equilibrium price = 6 zeds, where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied [1]
Equilibrium quantity = 50 thousand mangoes per week [1]
Excess demand at 4 zeds = 60 - 40 = 20 thousand mangoes per week [1]
questions.model_answer_note: Full marks need the equilibrium price and quantity plus the shortage with working and units.

questions.prompt: Beef and leather are in joint supply. A rise in the demand for beef in Kuva is most likely to lead to:
hints: Use the difference between joint supply and competitive supply.
Think about what happens to beef output, and what necessarily comes with it.
questions.targets: Joint supply: more of one means more of the other

options.text: a fall in the supply of leather
options.misconception: Producing more of one good means less of the other only in competitive supply.

options.text: a rise in the demand for leather
options.misconception: The link between beef and leather is on the production side, not the buyers' side.

options.text: an increase in the supply of leather
no change in the leather market
options.misconception: Because both goods come from the same animals, more beef output affects leather output.

questions.prompt: The price of electric scooters in Veld falls sharply. Using a demand and supply diagram for scooter helmets (described in words), explain the likely effect on the market for scooter helmets.
hints: Decide how scooters and helmets are related, and which curve in the helmet market this affects.
Trace the chain: scooter price, quantity of scooters bought, helmet demand, then the new helmet equilibrium.
questions.targets: Complements as a demand shifter and the new equilibrium
marking_points: Scooters and helmets are complements, so more scooters are bought when their price falls [1]
The demand for helmets increases, shown by a rightward shift of the demand curve [1]
The equilibrium price and quantity of helmets both rise [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer identifies the complement relationship, the direction of the demand shift and the effect on both price and quantity.

questions.prompt: In a competitive market with an upward-sloping supply curve, demand increases. What happens to the total revenue of the firms in the market?
hints: Total revenue is price multiplied by quantity sold.
On a demand and supply diagram, find what happens to both equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity after the shift.
questions.targets: Demand increase raises both P and Q, so revenue rises

options.text: It falls
options.misconception: Revenue would only fall if price or quantity fell, and neither does here.

options.text: It stays the same
options.misconception: Both price and quantity change in the same direction, so revenue cannot stay the same.

options.text: It may rise or fall depending on price elasticity of demand
options.misconception: Elasticity matters when a supply shift moves price and quantity in opposite directions, not for a demand shift.

options.text: It rises

questions.prompt: Table 3 shows the total product of a small furniture workshop in Tarsa in the short run. Calculate the marginal product of the third worker.

table.caption: Table 3: Output of a furniture workshop (chairs per week)

hints: Use the idea of marginal product and the rows for 2 and 3 workers in Table 3.
Find how much total product changes when the number of workers goes up by one.
questions.targets: Marginal product as a change in total product
marking_points: Working: 35 - 25 [1]
Marginal product of the third worker = 10 chairs per week [1]
questions.model_answer_note: Full marks need the correct subtraction and the answer with units; 35 (total product) scores 0.

questions.prompt: Mara is willing to pay up to 12 zeds for a concert ticket. She buys one for 8 zeds. What is her consumer surplus?
hints: Use the idea of consumer surplus.
Compare the most she would pay with what she actually paid.
questions.targets: Consumer surplus = willingness to pay minus price paid

options.text: 4 zeds
8 zeds
options.misconception: This is the price she paid, not the extra benefit she received.

options.text: 12 zeds
options.misconception: This is her maximum willingness to pay, not her surplus.

options.text: 20 zeds
options.misconception: Consumer surplus is a difference, not the sum of the two values.

questions.prompt: Floods destroy a large part of Kuva's rice crop. Using a demand and supply diagram (described in words), explain the effect on the market for rice.
hints: Decide which curve the floods affect and in which direction.
Describe what happens at the old price, how the market responds, and where it settles.
questions.targets: Supply shock: leftward shift, shortage, higher price
marking_points: The supply of rice decreases, shown by a leftward shift of the supply curve [1]
At the original price there is excess demand (a shortage), which pushes the price up [1]
The new equilibrium has a higher price and a lower quantity of rice [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer gives the direction of the shift, the adjustment through a shortage, and the new price and quantity.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the best example of bounded self-control?
hints: Use the three 'bounded' ideas and the common biases from behavioural economics.
Look for the person whose choice goes against a plan they had already made.
questions.targets: Recognising bounded self-control among other behavioural ideas

options.text: A shopper thinks a jacket is good value because its label shows a much higher 'original' price
options.misconception: Being influenced by a first number seen is anchoring.

options.text: A worker plans to save her bonus but spends it all on impulse the same day
A student gives money to charity even though it lowers her own spending
options.misconception: Acting to help others at a personal cost shows bounded selfishness.

options.text: A consumer picks a phone plan without comparing all the plans because there are too many
options.misconception: Limited ability to process information is bounded rationality.

questions.prompt: The demand curve for gym passes in Veld is a straight line. Table 4 shows three points on it. The market price rises from 8 zeds to 12 zeds. Calculate the fall in consumer surplus.

table.caption: Table 4: Points on the demand curve for gym passes
rows: Price at which quantity demanded is zero

hints: Consumer surplus is a triangle on the demand diagram, so use the formula for the area of a triangle.
Work out the triangle before and after the price rise using the top of the demand curve, then find the difference.
questions.targets: Consumer surplus as a triangle area and how it changes when price rises
marking_points: Fall in consumer surplus = 360 - 160 = 200 zeds [1]
questions.model_answer_note: Full marks need both triangle areas with working and the correct difference in zeds.

questions.prompt: Table 5 shows the supply of bicycles in Tarsa before and after a change. Which change is most likely to explain the data?

table.caption: Table 5: Quantity of bicycles supplied (per month)

hints: Compare the two quantity columns in Table 5 at each price.
Decide whether this is a movement along the supply curve or a shift, and in which direction, then match it to a cause.
questions.targets: Reading a supply shift from a schedule and linking it to a determinant

options.text: A rise in the price of bicycles
options.misconception: A price change moves along one supply schedule; here quantity rises at every price.

options.text: A rise in the wages of bicycle factory workers
options.misconception: Higher costs would lower quantity supplied at every price, not raise it.

options.text: An improvement in the technology used to make bicycles
An increase in consumers' demand for bicycles
options.misconception: A change in demand does not change the quantity firms will supply at each price.

questions.prompt: The demand for electric cars in Kuva rises. Explain how the price mechanism reallocates resources in response, referring to the signalling and incentive functions of price.
hints: Use the two functions of price in the price mechanism.
Start from the change in the price of electric cars, then say what information it gives and how producers and consumers respond.
questions.targets: Signalling vs incentive functions and resource reallocation
marking_points: The price of electric cars rises, signalling to producers that consumers want more of this good [1]
The price change passes information about a shortage to both buyers and sellers [1]
The higher price is an incentive for firms to produce more because it may raise profits (and for some consumers to buy less) [1]
So resources move towards making electric cars, the market where they are most wanted [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer explains both functions in the context of electric cars and ends with resources moving to the higher-valued use.

questions.prompt: A competitive market with no externalities is at equilibrium. Which statement is correct?
hints: Use the condition for allocative efficiency and the idea of social surplus.
Remember what the demand curve and supply curve each represent at the margin.
questions.targets: MB = MC at competitive equilibrium maximises social surplus

options.text: Marginal benefit equals marginal cost, so social surplus is maximised
Consumer surplus is at its highest possible level
options.misconception: Consumer surplus would be larger at a lower price; it is the sum of both surpluses that is maximised.

options.text: The price equals the highest price any consumer is willing to pay
options.misconception: Many consumers are willing to pay more than the equilibrium price, which is why consumer surplus exists.

options.text: Producer surplus is zero because firms sell at the market price
options.misconception: Most firms would accept less than the market price, so producer surplus is positive.

questions.prompt: Standard economic theory assumes consumers are rational and aim to maximise utility. Explain two reasons why consumers may not behave in this way.
hints: Use ideas from behavioural economics, such as the 'bounded' ideas and common biases.
For each reason, name the limit on the consumer and then show how it leads to a choice that does not give the most utility.
questions.targets: Limits of rationality applied to utility maximisation
marking_points: First reason identified, e.g. bounded rationality or imperfect information: consumers have limited information and limited ability to process it [1]
Explained: so they settle for a satisfactory choice (satisfice) rather than the utility-maximising one [1]
Second reason identified, e.g. bounded self-control or a bias such as anchoring or framing [1]
Explained: so they make choices, such as overspending or reacting to how a choice is presented, that do not maximise their utility [1]
questions.model_answer_note: Accept any two valid behavioural reasons; each needs to be named and linked to a non-maximising choice for 2 marks.

questions.prompt: Table 6 shows the average market price of cocoa in Kuva. Which statement about the data is correct?

table.caption: Table 6: Average price of cocoa in Kuva

hints: Use the price column in Table 6 and compare each year with the one before.
Check each statement against the numbers one at a time, including the size of each change.
questions.targets: Describing a price trend accurately from data

options.text: The price rose in every year shown
options.misconception: The price fell between 2023 and 2024.

options.text: The largest yearly rise in price was between 2022 and 2023
The price fell between 2022 and 2023
options.misconception: The price rose from 2.50 to 3.50 in that period.

options.text: The price in 2024 was double the price in 2021
options.misconception: The price rose from 2.00 to 3.00, which is 50% higher, not double.

questions.prompt: Global demand for oil falls as more countries switch to renewable energy. Using a demand and supply diagram (described in words), explain the effect on the total revenue of oil producers.
hints: Decide which curve moves, then use the formula for total revenue.
Find the new equilibrium price and quantity, then think about what happens when you multiply them.
questions.targets: Demand decrease lowers both P and Q, so revenue falls
marking_points: The demand curve for oil shifts to the left [1]
Equilibrium price and quantity of oil both fall [1]
Total revenue (price x quantity) therefore falls [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer gives the direction of the shift, the effect on both price and quantity, and links this to revenue.

questions.prompt: Firms in Tarsa automatically enrol all new workers in a pension savings plan, but workers can leave the plan at any time. Which type of choice architecture is this?
hints: Use the types of choice architecture: default, restricted and mandated choice.
Ask what happens to a worker who does nothing at all.
questions.targets: Recognising default choice (opt-out)

options.text: Default choice
Restricted choice
options.misconception: No options have been removed; workers can still leave the plan.

options.text: Mandated choice
options.misconception: Workers are not forced to make an active decision; the plan applies if they do nothing.

options.text: Anchoring
options.misconception: Anchoring is a bias from a first piece of information, not a way of designing choices.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between the short run and the long run in production.
hints: Think about the inputs a firm uses, such as labour, materials and factory buildings.
For each time period, say whether every input can be changed.
questions.targets: At least one fixed input vs all inputs variable
marking_points: The short run is a period in which at least one input (e.g. factory size) is fixed [1]
The long run is a period in which all inputs can be changed [1]
questions.model_answer_note: Full marks need the fixed-input idea for the short run and all-variable inputs for the long run; answers based only on calendar time get 0.

questions.prompt: On a demand and supply diagram of a competitive market at equilibrium, which area shows producer surplus?
hints: Use what the supply curve shows about the lowest price firms will accept.
Producer surplus compares that lowest acceptable price with the price firms actually receive, for the units sold.
questions.targets: Locating producer surplus on the diagram

options.text: The area below the demand curve and above the price
options.misconception: This area is consumer surplus.

options.text: The area below the supply curve up to the quantity sold
options.misconception: This area reflects firms' costs of production, not their surplus.

options.text: The area above the supply curve and below the price, up to the quantity sold
The whole area between the demand and supply curves up to the quantity sold
options.misconception: This area is social surplus, the sum of consumer and producer surplus.

questions.prompt: A school canteen in Veld wants students to eat more fruit but does not want to ban snacks or change prices. Explain how it could use choice architecture to do this.
hints: Use nudge theory and choice architecture.
Think about where and how foods are shown, why that affects what students pick, and what the canteen avoids doing.
questions.targets: Applying a nudge to a real setting
marking_points: It changes how the options are presented, e.g. placing fruit first in the line or at eye level and snacks further away [1]
Students often choose what is most visible or easiest to reach rather than weighing every option [1]
So more fruit is chosen while all options remain available and prices are unchanged (freedom of choice is kept) [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer gives a specific nudge, explains why it changes behaviour, and notes that choice is not restricted.

questions.prompt: Banks in Kuva start offering farmers loans at much lower interest rates. Using a demand and supply diagram for crops (described in words), explain the likely effect on the price of crops.
hints: Think about which side of the crop market cheaper loans affect, and which determinant is involved.
Trace the chain: cost of borrowing, what farmers do with the money, their costs or capacity, the curve, then the new equilibrium.
questions.targets: Cheaper credit as a supply-side determinant and its effect on price
marking_points: Lower interest rates reduce the cost of borrowing for farmers [1]
Farmers can invest in machinery or better inputs, lowering costs of production or raising capacity [1]
The supply curve of crops shifts to the right [1]
The equilibrium price of crops falls and the quantity rises [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer links cheaper credit to lower costs or more capacity, shows the rightward supply shift and states the fall in price.
